title: Slip-stitch checkers scarf
subtitle: A two-colour checkerboard pattern worked by slipping every other stitch.
excerpt: A scarf knitted flat in a two-colour slip-stitch checkerboard on 5 mm needles with aran-weight yarn, finishing at 20 cm wide by 155 cm long. The checkerboard effect is produced by alternating which stitches are slipped and which are worked on each two-row stripe, creating a graphic pattern without any stranding or intarsia.
sourceNotes: Slip-stitch colour patterns appear in Victorian knitting manuals including Weldon's Practical Knitter (1880s-1900s), Internet Archive. Checkerboard slip-stitch patterns are documented in many 19th-century fancy knitting collections.

glossaryTerms.definition: A two-colour technique in which one colour is worked for two rows, slipping the stitches that will show the other colour. Only one yarn is used at a time; the slipped stitches carry the colour upward without stranding.
A cast-on forming a neat elastic edge by using the tail and working yarn over two fingers simultaneously.

content.text: This is a scarf knitted flat in two-colour
slip-stitch colourwork

on 5 mm needles with aran-weight yarn, finishing at 20 cm wide and 155 cm long. Two colours alternate in pairs of rows; on each pair of rows, half the stitches are worked in the active colour and the other half are slipped, which carries the first colour upward. The alternation creates a graphic two-colour checkerboard. Only one yarn is in the hand at any time and there are no floats longer than one stitch.

This is classified BEGINNER because the only techniques are the knit stitch, the purl stitch, and slipping a stitch. The pattern repeat is four stitches and four rows, which is straightforward to memorise. The finished scarf needs about 190 m (approximately 110 g) each of aran-weight colour A and colour B.
What you need

items.name: Aran-weight yarn, colour A
items.substitutions: Any aran-weight yarn. High contrast between A and B gives the most graphic check.

items.name: 5 mm needles, straight or circular (UK 6 / US 8)

content.text: Gauge

18 sts x 24 rows = 10 x 10 cm in stocking stitch on 5 mm needles, blocked. In the slip-stitch checker pattern the gauge is approximately 16 sts per 10 cm and 28 rows per 10 cm because the slipped stitches widen the fabric slightly. One stitch per 10 cm off gauge shifts the finished width by approximately 1.25 cm.
Pattern
Cast on
Use the
long-tail cast-on

in colour A to place 32 stitches on the needle. The stitch count must be a multiple of 4 for the checker repeat. Before beginning, calculate the tail: tail_cm = (needle circumference mm x stitch count) / 10 + 15. For 5 mm needles (circumference approximately 15.7 mm) and 32 stitches: (15.7 x 32) / 10 + 15 = 50.2 + 15 = about 65 cm. Leave at least 65 cm of tail in colour A.
Stitch count check-in: after the cast-on you should have 32 stitches on the needle.
Body : 4-row repeat
Rows 1 and 2 are worked in colour A; rows 3 and 4 are worked in colour B. Both yarns hang at the right edge; do not cut between colour changes.
Row 1 (RS, colour A): *K2, sl2 purlwise wyib; repeat from * to end. (32 sts)
Row 2 (WS, colour A): *P2, sl2 purlwise wyif; repeat from * to end. (32 sts)
Row 3 (RS, colour B): *sl2 purlwise wyib, K2; repeat from * to end. (32 sts)
Row 4 (WS, colour B): *sl2 purlwise wyif, P2; repeat from * to end. (32 sts)
Repeat rows 1 to 4 until the scarf measures 155 cm. At the halfway mark (approximately row 217), count your stitches.
Stitch count check-in: at row 217 you should have 32 stitches on the needle.
Bind off
Work a standard bind-off on a row 1 or row 3 RS row in the active colour.
Common faults

Checker pattern shifting after a colour change. Rows 1 and 2 slip stitches 3 and 4 of each group; rows 3 and 4 slip stitches 1 and 2. Confusing rows 1 and 3 breaks the checkerboard alignment. At the start of each pair of rows, check which colour is active: A always works rows 1 and 2, B always works rows 3 and 4.

Yarn at the wrong side on slipped stitches. Wyib (with yarn in back) means yarn away from you; wyif (with yarn in front) means yarn toward you. If the yarn is on the wrong side for a slipped stitch, the float shows on the right side.

Edges tighter than the body. If the selvedge stitches of the two working colours both pull at the edge, carry the non-working yarn up the edge loosely every 4 rows by wrapping it around the working yarn before picking it up. This prevents a tight ladder at the right edge.
Finishing
Weave in all tails. The slip-stitch checker does not need blocking but can be lightly pressed on the WS with a damp cloth to flatten the fabric.
Care
Handwash in cool water with wool wash. Lay flat to dry.
What to try next
